speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our convenient affordable and well-connected transport system is Singapore's lifeblood.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is important that we can sustain the system's long-term both from an environmental and financial standpoint.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our ability to transform our public transport system depends on getting commuters on board.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Against our aim to move away from private transport and towards public transport and active mobility, a recent survey shows that there are still mixed opinions on the symbolic value of car ownership.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We need to further unpack and shape societal attitudes to realise our car-lite vision.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our Land Transport Masterplan 2040 also envisions cycling to be a mode of commute by which individuals can complete peak period journeys between home and work within 45 minutes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides building new cycling paths between towns, is it time to separate bicycle lanes on our roads, especially in the Central Business District.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I cycle around my constituency with my volunteers every weekend and I am aware that cyclists are sometimes made to feel unwelcome both by motorists on the roads and by pedestrians on roadside paths.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The quest for sustainable air and sea transport is a global one given the international nature of such activities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we explore low and zero-carbon fuels and other sustainability measures, we should look to collaborate with other countries in such endeavours.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have done well in ensuring our hub status in the air and the maritime sectors remain competitive globally but there are opportunities for us to gain more market share going forward and create good jobs at the same time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Are we on track and what does it mean for the Ministry of Transport (MOT) Budget and resource needs beyond 2023?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Pursuing these objectives will come at some cost.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our bus and rail services were already operating at a loss before the pandemic struck.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must strike a balance between ensuring that the funding gap does not unsustainably widen and managing the cost impact on commuters is key.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, we also need to balance spending on ensuring upgrades to our transport infrastructure and safety checks are there to meet our sustainability targets and possibly gradual changes may be needed to ensure the market microstructure of our pricing mechanisms to control vehicle population remains up-to-date with the sustainability changes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: All these are not easy as we also face at the same time external shocks or factors affecting prices going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As such I would like to ask MOT in pursuing our environmental and financial sustainability targets and strategies, what will be the impact on the cost for commuters and Singaporeans at large?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: EV chargers are being installed in HDB multi-storey car parks and public spaces to provide accessible charging infrastructure across the island.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: And what will be the considerations for the charging fee model for EV chargers installed in public premises?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the plans for existing petrol and diesel pump stations as more drivers switch to EVs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What has been the average utilisation rate for current public EV charging stations?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: New charging stations will be rolled out in all HDB carparks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How many EV vehicles and motorcycles can these additional EV stations in each HDB carpark support?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has introduced a series of initiatives to encourage and support EV adoption.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government provide an update on some of the key initiatives, including the EV Charging Act and the EV Common Charger Grant?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Are we on track in terms of the rate of EV charger deployment and EV adoption?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first requires a computation based on car’s power rating.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second is a figure to be added, called the additional annual fixed component (AAFC).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This has caused some unhappiness among EV owners due to the weakness of the principle behind imposing the AAFC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MOT stressed then that the AAFC was not punitive but was an interim measure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, some EV owners find it punitive as the AAFC arbitrarily raises their road tax by as much as one-third despite the whole-of-Government avowed push towards green policies and clean energy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I understood from the Budget Statement in 2020 that the end game for road tax on EVs is distance-based charging using the next-generation Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) system.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, in a Parliamentary answer to Member of Parliament Mr Louis Chua in 2021, the Government stated that it was studying different approaches and options for distance-based charging that were fuel independent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Would the Ministry clarify what this means exactly?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: First of all, I would like to declare my interest as the President of Strides Mobility Services, a subsidiary of SMRT Corporation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But we need to peel the onion further to understand the composition of the EVs registered last year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In particular, we hope MOT can reveal how many of the EVs were registered as passenger cars under COE Cat A and Cat B respectively.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How many of the EV-registered vehicles were commercial vehicles and motorcycles?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I supposed electric cars and electric commercial vehicles users face different sets of challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What is MOT's plan to encourage EV adoption in passenger cars and commercial vehicles respectively?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: In addition, could MOT share the EV adoption rate among the Government vehicles?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What is the Government's plan to adopt EVs across the different Government departments?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Is there a centralised plan or is each Ministry responsible for their EV adoption or conversion plan by themselves?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, we know that there is an overwhelming majority of public buses that are running on diesel engines.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Is LTA accelerating the purchase of electric buses?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: How many electric buses is LTA buying this year and next year?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: What are the challenges in running electric buses?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Are electric buses more costly to acquire and run?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: If so, will that translate to higher bus fares?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: On the other hand, there are also opportunities to run EVs at the airport and seaport as the range anxiety is less of an issue in the confined space of the airports and seaports.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Would MOT update us on the electrification plan at the airports and seaports?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Will the Ministry consider expediting the conversion of our public buses to electric buses?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are the main challenges facing the conversion process?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Currently Kaki Bukit ward is being served by bus services 225G, 225W, 137 and 137A.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Buses 225G and 225W are feeder services, starting and ending at Bedok Interchange and they cover the loop of Bedok North Avenue 1, Avenue 2 and Street 3, each going in the opposite direction.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I understand from residents that these two feeder services have been around since the early days of Kaki Bukit estate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Bus service 137A, which is a short-trip service variant of bus service 137 was introduced in February 2019.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Bus service 137A only operates on weekday mornings to cater to peak hours commuting, making a total of four trips – first at 7.18 am and final at 8.07 am.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of the common feedback received is to enhance the connectivity of the feeder services serving Kaki Bukit to wider parts of Bedok North, Bedok South and also Bedok Reservoir by introducing Townlink feeder service.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Such a service can be found in some HDB towns such as Pasir Ris.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Many who had called for this mentioned that such Townlink feeder service will, in particular, benefit groups with different mobility needs, such as the elderly, persons with disabilities and families with young children because it will do away with the hassle of bus transfers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: There are also requests to increase the frequency for bus services 137 and 137A during peak hours.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The feedback is that these services is often crowded and impossible to board, especially for residents taking the bus services from the last three stops away from the Downtown Line, Bedok North station bus stop.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: During the morning peak travel hours, residents have to compete to get on the buses and the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) to the Central Business District (CBD).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry consider providing more direct city bus services during the peak hours?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry consider a feasibility study for an extension of the Cross Island Line to extend from Punggol West to support residents at Jalan Kayu and Yio Chu Kang Road, as well as Fernvale?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: They are especially in need of MRT access to travel to other parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The construction of the Downtown and Thomson-East Coast Lines greatly enhances accessibility across our island.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Minister provide an update on these lines?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What is the average ridership for both the Downtown and Thomson-East Coast Lines so far?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If all public buses are operating on EV mode, would this help reduce the costs of operating the buses as there would be substantial savings in fuel?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: That would require our public transport system to be accessible and affordable, safe, reliable, clean and comfortable, and not overcrowded.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With six MRT and three LRT lines in operation, what are the annual operation and maintenance expenses?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Also, with the recent increase in fuel prices and electricity tariffs, what is the increase in annual operation and maintenance expenses for public buses?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: To cope with the rising costs of operation and maintenance, what is the expected fare revenue that will be collected from commuters from MRT and bus ridership?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With the return to DORSCON Green, public transport ridership has largely recovered, what is the projected annual Government subsidy that is still required in order to ensure a safe, reliable, accessible and affordable public transportation system?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In addition to our MRT and public bus services, commuters have the options of taxis or private hire cars.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: With the convenience of almost instant matching on mobile apps, point-to-point transport services have never been more popular.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the availability of P2P drivers?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What are its plans in the event of a shortage?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: However, the report also revealed that the wait times were less satisfactory.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Acknowledging that there can never be such anything such as a "perfect" system, I have to make three points.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: First, I would like to ask MOT how it intends to improve P2P service waiting times.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Second, it is good that the PTC has expanded the scope of research to persons with disabilities (PwDs) and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Important service attributes that PwDs identified to include in Singapore's public transport system are reliability, safety and security, and accessibility.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: I want to ask MOT how it has taken the data collected from the PTC Survey to enhance the experience of PwDs and their caregivers.

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Can MOT also share its plans to improve the user experience of the elderly to achieve its objective of providing a sound transport system?

speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
text: Third, I would like to ask MOT to share more about its plan to increase awareness and growth of the Caring SG Commuters movement, which promotes courteous behaviour, such as giving up seats for the elderly, pregnant women and PwDs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The past three years have taken a long toll on our taxi and private-vehicle-hire drivers, with many drivers having disrupted livelihoods, depleted savings and sometimes, battered mental and physical health.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While endemic living has given some form of reprieve to our P2P community, they remain worried about their future and their livelihoods, due to an ageing driving workforce, the ever-widening MRT coverage, the roll-out of EVs and rising costs of business.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I have brought these issues up previously in this House and I seek an update on the Ministry's considerations.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will also help alleviate the retirement pressures that many are feeling, especially after the three-year pandemic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Vehicles are key to our P2P livelihoods and rentals can often eat into more than 50% of a driver's revenues.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Very often too, renters are asked to sign onerous rental agreements which must include vehicle insurance that can bear unequitable terms, such as high excess sums.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We call on the Ministry to work with the Labour Movement to look into the pressing issue of setting out fair practice guidelines for the rental of vehicles used for trade.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our P2P community has also brought up the growth of a grey economy, ride sharing or car-pooling – a practice which lies on the fringes of what can be considered not legal P2P ride-hail travel.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the past year, this community has grown, and at last count, on just one online chat channel, there are 200,000 participants.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has impacted the livelihoods of our drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can Ministry share on what measures have been taken or will be taken to address these issues?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our P2P drivers are excited to join Singaporeans in a sustainable green future and are keen to make the shift to EVs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the rollout speeds and norms of charging point use are top of the mind for drivers and the Labour Movement and our P2P associations call for priority use of charging points for drivers who use vehicles for livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We also call for more support for our early adopters as they will be expected to take on more costs due to a nascent EV ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: This option fills a demand gap in serving the needs of public transport commuters who require the use of a private vehicle occasionally.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is MOT's assessment of the effectiveness of the car sharing option as an alternative to car ownership?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Has MOT implemented programmes or incentives that would help car sharing companies scale up their operations to enhance the attractiveness and increase the accessibility of this mode of transportation?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry consider formalising the framework for this sector to ensure nationwide coverage by the various companies, as well as the availability of different types of vehicles, such as those that can accommodate wheelchairs, so that more people facing difficulties using public transport can be served?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Demand continues to be high since last year's COS debate and measures implemented in March 2002 have only provided temporary respite.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: We must identify the specific drivers of this persistent and strong motorcycle demand to effectively address the soaring COE premiums.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Will there be a need to review bid deposits much higher, possibility to $2,000 and shorten the validity period?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Is the Ministry and LTA looking at other market microstructure measures on the retail side to reduce demand?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Considering the value of motorcycles to delivery services and to lower income Singaporeans who rely on motorcycles for their livelihoods, what are the Ministry's plans to ensure motorcycle COE supply remains adequate and affordable going forward?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Parking and environmental sustainability are possibly some other reasons behind maintaining the zero-percent growth rate for motorcycles until January 2025.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But these issues can be targeted in other ways and not just by constricting the number of motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As the COE and vehicle quota system are mainly to control traffic congestion, is there room for calibrated marginal increase in motorcycle quotas, whether by creation or reallocation from other categories, as motorcycles do not take up as much traffic space as cars?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A Bloomberg article late last year put it aptly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore's reputation as one of the world's most expensive cities now extends to one of its cheapest modes of transportation: motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many Singaporeans who earn wages at the lower deciles rely on motorcycles for transport, gig work or undertaking deliveries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In response to last year's changes, the Motorcycle Trade Association suggested raising the COE bid deposit to $2,000 and reducing the COE validity period to one month.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry share if it has looked at this to further manage motorcycles COE premiums?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, an important but seldom discussed aspect of high motorcycle COE prices revolves around the largely unregulated motorcycle financing ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact here is that it is the motorcycle traders and sellers that overwhelmingly offer in-house financing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In some cases, the interest-bearing component of such loans can be oppressive for our motorcyclists.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: High COE prices mean motorcyclists will require more financing to buy motorcycles.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There have been concerns expressed about how the prospect of offering such financing in and of itself provide an opportunity to profit from financing, even if a motorcycle is prematurely returned before the loan is fully settled since the unused portion of the COE can be redeemed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Do high COE prices for motorcycles create a perverse incentive for some motorcycle finances to drive up motorcycles COE prices in a largely unregulated space?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would MOT look at motorcycle finance as an area of deep study and review to ensure that motorcycle riders – almost 70% of whom ride Class 2B motorcycles and who are more than likely earning well below the median income – are not unfairly penalised because of a lack of Government regulation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: On 1 January this year, the Government rolled out new rules to improve the safety of workers ferried in the rear decks of lorries.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Measures included a designated vehicle buddy and a requirement to ensure that drivers must be well-rested if they happen to be a worker too.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Migrant worker groups, however, have continued to highlight that these do not adequately address the core issue that transporting workers on lorries, where heavy equipment and human passengers co-mingle, is fundamentally unsafe.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This presents us an opportunity to phase out lorries that are currently approved to ferry passengers on the rear deck but without the proper safety measures installed.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Can MOT consider revising the lorry homologation process so that only those that can allow for proper seats and proper seat belts to be installed in rear decks can be sold in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By doing so, we can gradually refresh our lorry fleets without imposing additional costs on business owners.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: We understand that LTA has plans to build cycling paths to reach 1,300 kilometres by 2030.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: From LTA's website, we can see that most of the cycling paths are concentrated in the central, northern and eastern parts of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In contrast, there are very few cycling paths in the western part of Singapore with the exception of cycling paths around Jurong Lake and Bukit Panjang.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: In Nanyang Division, for example, many residents feedback to me that we have many cyclists but there are no cycling paths that are built by LTA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Based on the LTA's current plan, how many kilometres of cycling path would LTA build this year and next year?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: How many towns, like Nanyang, do not have any dedicated cycling paths built by LTA as of now?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: What would it take to accelerate the construction of cycling paths?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, many more Singaporeans started to cycle and used the Park Connectors Network (PCN).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: As the champion for green transport, I hope MOT or LTA can ride on the momentum to accelerate the construction of cycling paths to reduce carbon emission and promote healthy living at the same time.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides space constraint on our road network, this is another measure to ensure road safety, an area that I feel strongly about in safeguarding lives.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While there has been a positive increase in the popularity of cycling during the COVID-19 pandemic, we have also seen a spike in the number of traffic accidents involving cyclists.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am a keen supporter of cycling as a great sport to keep healthy but prefer that there be a dedicated cycling track separated from drivers and pedestrians as far as possible for safety reasons.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my Jalan Kayu Constituency, there is a stretch of vacant land, along Yio Chu Kang Road, on the south and Sengkang West Road on the east, that can be developed with dedicated cycling path all the way to the beautiful Seletar Aerospace area.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Some cycle as a means of transport while others cycle for recreation and sports using the PCN and roadways.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: To enhance safety for pedestrians, can LTA bring forward, in all towns, the construction of dedicated bicycle paths to improve the first and last mile connectivity, from MRT stations?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: For shared paths within a certain radius from an MRT station, there is usually a higher density of both cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Dedicated cycling paths and pedestrian paths between MRT stations and the next major junction would help to segregate traffic and improve safety, especially during the morning and evening peak periods.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While I applaud the enforcement efforts of the LTA officers and I appreciate that we have come a long way from the heyday the e-scooter menace.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many people are still using their e-scooters illegally despite the enforcement and public education efforts.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Our Enforcement Officers cannot be at every street, junction or footpath.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I still see e-scooters being used almost every day on footpaths or on the roads.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Though allowed, most houses or flats are not directly linked to a Park Connector and how often do we see anyone pushing their e-scooters along footpaths, enroute to Park Connectors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We also read of fires from charging e-scooters which imply continual use.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The restrictions on e-scooters led to the rise in the number of electric bikes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: E-bikes are not allowed on footpaths, yet many are still being used on footpaths.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have seen them on HDB void decks too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the roads, it is comments to common to see some e-bike riders —

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Delivery riders rough it out, rain or shine, night or day, to keep logistical networks in Singapore alive in the new normal, be it courier services, food delivery or other forms of logistics.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Unfortunately, in a normal course of their work, our delivery riders sometimes have really bad odds stacked against them, causing them their livelihoods and sometimes, in extreme, even their limbs and their lives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our riders have given the feedback that due to them using bicycles and power-assisted rides for delivery, they are often in no man's land.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: When on pathways, they share the space with pedestrians and many pedestrians are on their headsets or seniors and young children with slower reaction times.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: When on roads, they share the space with cars, buses and other heavy vehicles.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: While rules have been put into place to help protect our riders, example, the 1.5 metres distance when overtaking.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: When the rubber hits the road, literally, our riders stand no chance in a collision with a vehicle.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: No doubt gracious, pathway and road sharing is important to cultivate.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: And I ask the Ministry to provide an update on what programmes would be put in place to give awareness to all stakeholders on sharing norms.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: In addition, in areas where there's no possibility of broadening out pathways, how will the Ministry look to demarcate their use?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This includes the bicycle, additional batteries, delivery items and the frame used to carry the items for delivery.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our riders are given the feedback that this 20-kilogram limit causes them to compromise on safety, for example, taking on the lightest bike frame and this can lead to instability with a full delivery load and of course, bumpy road conditions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Our riders appreciate the 20-kilogram safety feature for pathways but are very worried about the risk they take on the road.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Residents often narrate to me their near-miss encounters with bicycles and mobility devices on footpaths and cycling paths. "I wonder whether a short trip on foot to our neighbourhood amenities, such as the polyclinic, stadium, or local hawker centre these days, can really be safe!", some lament.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With our foot- and cycling-path sharing culture between various user groups admittedly still in its infancy, what can we do to ensure that even as we nudge changes in behaviour in our last mile commute, we do not do so at the expense of the safety of our residents?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Would people in a rush be willing to wait for passengers who are less mobile to board the bus or train?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Would a more inclusive transport system also means higher costs and what is the vision of inclusive transport system by MOT?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: If it is more costly to have an inclusive transport system, would it translate to higher transport fares?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Many citizens feel that public transport must be affordable, reliable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: For non-car owners who may need private transport due to the need to ferry young children or the elderly parents, they have seen a spike in hire car charges.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: Hence, they worry that substitute options like taxis and private car hire are getting more expensive.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: What are the expectations of Singaporeans for our public transport system?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: These pedestrians-only streets have become very leisurely stretches where people can connect with each other and engage in community activities together.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The placemaking of these pedestrianised stretches have also given these spots a new identity and attractiveness.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the lessons learnt from the first few pilots of converting streets into pedestrians-only ones?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Beyond the central regions and tourists areas, are there plans to extend such pedestrians-only streets into the heartlands' town centres?

text: I understand that the LTA is studying how Singapore's road infrastructure, can better support walking and cycling in neighbourhood centres to create a more livable and inclusive environment for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: This includes the pedestrianisation of roads or the creation of wider foot and cycling paths.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Punggol is home to many young families and to beautiful waterways and park connectors.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling
text: Cycling has always been a favourite activity of families and our youths and our Punggol residents have asked if we would be introducing new innovative concepts to our roads and pathways to promote community bonding and healthier lifestyles, especially for our seniors and youths.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: For Tanjong Pagar, MOT sought inputs from the local community and carried out a number of enhancement works.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: These works include enlargement of walkways, introduction of new zebra crossings, new road islands to facilitate pedestrian crossings, traffic calming features and also a cycling route through the area.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: I am aware of this because I am a member of Discover Tanjong Pagar, a local business association.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Such works are not iconic and do not draw much attention nor publicity.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: However, they are what matters on a day-to-day basis, in enhancing the experience of pedestrians and commuters.

speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on its effort to enhance walkability and whether any new areas are being considered for such enhancement projects?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the earlier Budget debate, I shared that in order for Singapore to become a nation Made for Families, our infrastructure needs to be ready to cater to the needs of families with young children as far as our seniors and those with mobility issues.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Improving the accessibility of this group of people to allow for them to travel to places they frequent, is important.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To achieve that, installing lifts to our pedestrian overhead bridges and ensuring that the surrounding areas are sheltered with barrier-free access, are critical.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One example is the overhead bridge Woodgrove Zone 7, connecting Woodgrove residents to Marsiling Mall, Woodland Sports Complex and PCF Marsiling Mega Centre and for Marsiling residents to travel to the family Service Centre in Woodgrove.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many seniors residing in Zone 7 have shared that they would often get their meals and groceries from Marsiling Mall hawker centre and supermarket just across the road.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding that there is a traffic light crossing a few hundred metres away, if given a choice, they would prefer to take the bridge as a safer option, especially during wet weather.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Unfortunately, the sad reality is that many of them when carrying their heavy groceries, find it, almost an impossible task to walk up to overhead bridge.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some had no choice but to resort to jay walking across the road from under the bridge during wet weather especially.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Similar feedback were also received from parents of young children, as they struggle to get across to the infant care preschool, as well as for swimming lessons whenever they travel with prams.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The Caring SG Commuters movement first began in August 2017 with the aim of growing a caring commuting culture.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Commuters may also have, over time, become good travel buddies with the "thoughtful bunch" on our public transport system: #StandUpStacey, #BagDownBenny, #HushHushHannah, #MoveInMartin and #GiveWayGlenda.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Further efforts to create a caring commuting culture was crystallised when the Caring SG Commuters committee was formed in 2020.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The committee's mandate was to "facilitate and pull together multi-agency efforts in the ideation, implementation and publicity of initiatives that transforms our public transport system and commuting culture, into one that is more caring, welcoming and inclusive." Over the past few years, we have kept at our efforts in engendering a more caring commuter culture.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: In 2021, the Caring Commuter Week was launched.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: The Outstanding Caring Commuter Award, which was recently renamed the Richard Magnus Award for the Outstanding Commuter, recognises nominees for their acts of care and kindness.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: These are but a few examples of what has been done to change mindsets and nudge behaviour.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Yet, we hear stories which suggest that inclusivity remains a stretch goal when it comes to our public transport system experience.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Paralympic swimmer Sophie Soon and her guide dog’s experience in November last year, was instructive.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Sophie is visually impaired and relies on Orinda, her guide dog, in getting from point to point.

speaker: Mr Eric Chua
text: Considering these developments, can MOT and LTA share plans for evolving and extending the Caring SG Commuters movement, so that Singapore's public transport system can truly be one that is caring and inclusive?

text: Given the necessity of our port workers to be on site 24/7, the introduction of thousands more workers to the Tuas area, can the Ministry provide an update to the transport options available to our port workers, especially last mile connectivity such as MRT, LRT and other P2P transport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First, the digitalisation of services or operations can help reduce costs amid rising prices and interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Various practical, digital solutions to reduce manual, lower-value work, are proposed in the Singapore Shipping Associations Maritime digitalisation playbook and the Industry Digital Plans or IDPs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: IDPs are presently available for sub-sectors like bunkering, harbour craft and ship agency and I wonder if more sub-sectors will soon be covered.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second, digitalisation can facilitate better connectivity and integration within an ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Is there a progress update on the harmonisation of APIs and data standards across different ports under digital oceans?

text: And what are the Ministry's digitalisation plans for the maritime sector, considering businesses uptake of digitalisation solutions and schemes, thus far?

text: The maritime sector is digitalisation will also increase the risk of exposure to cyber threats.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Malicious actors may launch cyber attacks to steal valuable data for ransom, sabotage critical operations and infrastructure to damage Singapore's reputation, orr a concealed illicit activity that utilises our seaport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: SMEs are also unlikely to have the knowledge to synchronise its cyber defences with existing protection such as the Singapore Maritime Cyber Security Operations Centre which provides early detection, monitoring and response to cyber attacks.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We are a global hub port and international maritime centre, and is consistently ranked top by international publications.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: During the COVID years, the maritime industry is one of the bright spots for Singapore's battled economy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: With our strong foundation, Singapore can and should continue to play an important role in global trade.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, the world is changing quickly, spurred on by technology, the sustainability imperative and changing geopolitics.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore’s Maritime Industry needs to evolve in tandem if we are to remain relevant.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First, we must remain an open economy that offers a safe and stable environment that sets us apart from the rest.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, the Government announced plans for Tuas Port.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister provide an update on the progress of the construction of the port?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Second, we must embrace innovation and, in fact, accelerate the pace to distance ourselves from competition.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: TradeNet put Singapore on the world map in the 1980s.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: SGTraDex has the promise of doing the same in this millennium.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And, of course, we need to have the talent, both local and global, to continue to lead the industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How does the Ministry plan to attract talented Singaporeans in this sector and ensure they are equipped with the right skills?

text: Ms Poh Li San, take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our aviation and maritime hubs are amongst the leading global hubs.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: They also generate significant carbon emissions due to the reliance on fossil fuels to power the aircraft and ships.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: On the bright side, Changi Airport has been consistently rated not only as one of the world’s best airports but also one of the most environmentally-friendly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It is lauded for its skylights, abundance of greenery, energy-efficient motion sensors and lighting, water-efficient fittings and roof-mounted solar panels.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Singapore remains in top position as the world's busiest container transshipment port, but we may not be amongst the most sustainable ones.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: According to a 2020 study of 36 seaports selected from North America, Europe (EU) and Asia Pacific, EU seaports had adopted more sustainability initiatives, compared to North American and Asia Pacific seaports.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What is the strategy for both sectors to support our national 2050 net-zero domestic emissions target?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the pathway, policies and regulations that will be put in place to incentivise sustainability measures?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can research institutes, industry MNCs, financial institutes and regulatory bodies work together to co-create solutions for decarbonisation?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can existing infrastructure and assets be adapted to reduce their carbon footprint to prevent them from becoming stranded assets?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: And what are the strategic international framework and partnership established so far in bilateral agreements to catalyse our transition?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The global aviation industry has undergone dramatic upheavals throughout the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Passenger traffic on Singapore Airlines and at Changi Airport have rebounded sharply over the past year since our borders opened in April 2022.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With the Chinese borders fully opened recently, how is our aviation industry poised for further growth and how can our air hub emerge even stronger than before the pandemic, considering the uneven recovery of other global and regional air hubs?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: On the other hand, what are the key challenges facing the aviation industry as it rides on this wave of recovery?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: The airlines and airports suffered severe financial losses in the past three years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Given the strong demand, is there headroom to increase airport charges to recover the losses and to cushion against higher operating costs due to energy and manpower cost increases?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What kind of assistance is the Ministry providing to support the recovery?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: The opening of Chinese borders will, hopefully, lead to resumption of most of our pre-COVID-19 flights with China.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: As air travel resumes and continues to grow in the coming months, especially with the possibility of Changi returning to pre-COVID-19 level flights, I would like to ask the Minister now for an update on the Government's plans for the building of T5.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: I would also like to ask whether there are any lessons we have learnt from the last three years of uncertainty caused by the pandemic which we can and would be applying to our T5 design and plans.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Were any of these works halted at any time during the pandemic?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: China's decision to reopen its borders to quarantine-free international travel in 2023 means we can expect the number of China-Singapore flights to multiply.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This was swiftly followed by our decision to move from DORSCON Yellow to Green which removed some of the last travel restrictions of non-vaccinated travellers entering Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I look forward to hearing more concrete plans and timelines for the construction of T5.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Do we now have enough information and data to decide how we intend to proceed or are we going to adopt a wait-and-see stance for a while?

text: Our aviation hub status is not just defined by size or quantity, but quality as well.

text: The rapid post-COVID-19 recovery of our aviation sector has seen labour shortages, after workers that left the aviation sector for other sectors amidst the one- to two-year standstill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: As we ramp up recruitment to ease capacity constraints, we must ensure that these workers are suitably familiarised and trained in airport operations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Some of these hires are newcomers to the industry and not workers who have taken a break during the COVID-19 period and are returning to familiar jobs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The coming years will be interesting times for the aviation sector.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Airlines and other industry operators will have to contend with rocketing costs, including energy prices.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, can the Ministry provide an update on the recovery of our aviation hub and what new competition it is currently and likely to face in the future?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Are there plans even for Terminal 6 or Terminal 7?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But that is probably way in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: So, what is the Government's outlook for the sector over the next year and the resource constraints that are likely to remain unchanged?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Whilst the increasing passenger volume and the aviation sector recovery will be good news to most, I would like to ask the Government some questions.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Two, how is the manpower growth in Changi Airport matching up with the recovery pace to ensure that our airport frontline and operations staff can cope with the increasing volume?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Three, as the advisor to DNATA Singapore's Staff Union, I would like to know how the Government will ensure the welfare and safety of more than 1,000 staff providing the full range of aviation security and ground-handling services who will also be managing increasing volume?

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling
text: Lastly, as the aviation industry is a major contributor to carbon emission, how is the Government enabling more sustainable solutions, like the conversion to low carbon fuels, to align with Singapore's commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050?

text: In fact, the International Air Transport Association has projected that Asia Pacific will be the fastest-growing region for air travel in the next two decades.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, I would like to thank all the Members who persevered till 8.00 pm last night to speak on the Budget of the Ministry of Transport (MOT).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And many have made it back to the Chamber this morning.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In responding to Members' questions and suggestions, my colleagues, Ms Amy Khor, Mr Chee Hong Tat, Mr Baey Yam Keng and I will elaborate on how my Ministry is working to build a resilient, sustainable and inclusive transport sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: My response will focus on three broad themes: recovery, growth and sustainability; and our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our air and land transport sectors have recovered strongly from the debilitating impact of the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At its lowest point in 2020, Changi's passenger traffic was less than 0.5% of pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To Mr Gan Thiam Poh's query, flights at Seletar have fully recovered since January this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One determinant, as Ms Ng Ling Ling noted, would be how quickly air connectivity with China is restored.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Weekly services to China have more than doubled since January, from 38 to nearly 100.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That is about a quarter of the number we had in 2019, with Chinese and Singapore carriers expected to resume even more services in the coming months.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about our aviation hub's challenges amidst the recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, our aviation stakeholders must continue to ramp up their workforce to sustain the recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, the sector's workforce is at about 90% of pre-COVID-19 levels and we expect a full recovery by this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But beyond recruitment, we must ensure that the new hires gain the requisite experience to meet the demands of the job and, also, to ensure their safety, welfare and morale, as Ms Ng Ling Ling has highlighted.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, though Singapore is in now in Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Green, we must remain alert to new threats from the virus and other similar threats.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are, therefore, closely monitoring the situation with the Ministry of Health (MOH) and must be prepared to respond quickly should the public health risk assessment change.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Third, the recovery of air travel will have to contend with uncertainties in the global economy and rising energy and manpower costs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Against this backdrop, Ms Poh had asked if there was room for airport charges to be raised.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Last September, the Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) and the Changi Airport Group (CAG) announced increases to the airport charges for passengers and airlines.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will review these charges periodically, so that CAAS and CAG can continue to invest in capacity building and essential infrastructure, while ensuring Changi remains competitive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Turning to land transport, our public transport ridership reached 90% of pre-COVID-19 levels in January this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Public transport journeys to the Downtown Core in the morning peak are at about 70%; whereas journeys to other areas, like Queenstown, are at 90%; and Woodlands and Tuas are already back to pre-COVID-19 levels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are tracking these travel patterns, which have yet to stabilise because of various adjustments to work practices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our maritime hub was resilient and performed well through the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More recently, due to global economic headwinds, international container trade and container freight rates have softened from the exceptionally high levels of 2021, but the mid- to long-term outlook remains positive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Overall, our air, sea and land transport sectors are back on track.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Capitalising on the recovery, as well as learning from the pandemic, we are now gearing up for growth.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have three priorities – capacity, capability and sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, a core focus of my Ministry is to invest in our transport infrastructure capacity to meet future needs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To Mr Gan Thiam Poh's query, these lines will have several points of intersections with our existing rail network, thereby enhancing the resilience of the system and convenience for commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our land connectivity with Malaysia will improve with the Johor Bahru-Singapore Rapid Transit System Link, which is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As for Mr Gan's question about a possible high-speed rail (HSR) link, I would like to reiterate what we have said before, that Singapore remains open to discussing any new proposal from Malaysia, starting from a clean slate.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Dennis Tan sought an update on Terminal 5 (T5).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: At last year's National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lee announced that we have restarted the T5 project.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Land preparation and drainage works at Changi East have been completed, and construction is expected to commence by 2025.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The third runway will also be ready towards the later part of this decade.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As shared by Deputy Prime Minister Wong in his Budget round-up speech, it is important that we set aside some resources whenever we have the means for projects with large and lumpy expenditure.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Meanwhile, the CAG and airport stakeholders have worked out operational plans to manage the anticipated growth in flights and passengers at Changi in the run-up to T5.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, to strengthen our capabilities, we will invest in our workforce, redesign jobs and deepen skillsets.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our upcoming rail lines will create about 800 good jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will use the Rail Manpower Development Incentive to equip our workers for these jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More than 2,900 have already been trained in skills, such as data analytics and condition-based monitoring since 2020.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This year, we are committing a further $12 million to this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Attracting talent to the aviation and maritime sectors is a key thrust as highlighted by Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are collaborating with our partners to do so through student outreach and work-study programmes, mid-career conversions and skills upgrading for workers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will also provide career guidance and employability support through touchpoints, such as the OneAviation Careers Hub portal.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee will elaborate on our plans for the maritime sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Thirdly, Mr Chairman, sustainability is central to the growth of our transport sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hence, we have partnered the industry to develop sustainability pathways in all three domains.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Last year, I highlighted our plans to drive electrification in the land transport sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We made good progress in 2022 with Electric Vehicles (EVs) accounting for 11.8% of new car registrations last year, up from 3.8% in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Of all EVs registered in 2022, 20% were from Category A (Cat A), 50% from Cat B and 30% from Cat C.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have announced that diesel cars and taxis cannot be registered for use from 2025, nor Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) cars and taxis from 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, we have financial incentives to encourage the adoption of EVs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked why EVs incur an Additional Flat Component.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As the then-Minister for Finance explained in Budget 2020, fuel excise duties are significant contributors to Government revenue, yielding around $1 billion annually.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Additional Flat Component for EVs – of $700 a year – was introduced to partly account for this loss in fuel excise duties.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: By way of comparison, a typical ICE car user will pay about $1,000 a year of fuel excise duties, assuming that they use the 92 or 95 octane petrol.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Separately, the total cost of ownership for EVs has been reduced through Government initiatives, such as the EV Early Adoption Incentive and the reduction in road tax for mass-market EVs, our adjustments in power-rating.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will continue to review road tax as part of the overall vehicular tax structure, taking into account the transition to electric, as well as other cleaner energy vehicles and technological developments, while staying true to our objectives of controlling private vehicle ownership and usage.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Thirdly, we have brought forward the islandwide deployment of EV chargers to address range anxiety.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: One in three Housing and Development Board (HDB) carparks will have EV charging points by the end of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We have also supported the installation of EV chargers in private developments through legislative amendments and the EV Common Charger Grant.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Khor will give more details.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our efforts to green the public transport sector are also gathering pace.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: New bus depots will be completed in tandem to support e-bus operations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will help achieve the goal of electrifying half our bus fleet by 2030 and a 100% cleaner-energy bus fleet by 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Several Members asked about the cost impact of switching to e-buses.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are in the early stages of electrifying our bus fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: But based on the experience of the e-bus fleet trial, the higher upfront costs are expected to be offset by lower-operating costs in the long run.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I should also add that, as announced at the launch of GreenGov.SG in July 2021, from this year, all new cars procured by the public sector will be electric, or alternatives with zero tailpipe emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Electrification will also be a key lever to reduce domestic emissions in our air and sea transport sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Currently, close to 20% of around 2,500 airside vehicles at Changi Airport are electric.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We want all vehicles on the airside to run on cleaner energy by 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This would include electrification or the use of biofuels.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To drive this transition, we will embark on three initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, we will enhance the charging infrastructure on the airside.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To date, CAG has installed about 100 EV charging stations, and this will increase to more than 300 over the next few years, in tandem with the needs of its airport partners as they electrify their airside fleet.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Third, we will commence trials on the use of renewable diesel, especially for specialised airport ground handling vehicles for which there are no electric models.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These trials will inform our evaluation of renewable diesel as a complement to electrification, to achieve the goal of cleaner airside vehicles by 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This will apply to about 1,600 harbour craft currently licensed by the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MPA will partner industry, financial institutions, harbour craft operators and manufacturers to help lower the cost of adoption and mobilise support for early adopters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MPA will launch an Expression of Interest (EOI) in the second quarter of this year to call for proposals for the design and development, demand aggregation and green financing for new electric harbour craft.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The pleasure craft sector and domestic tugboats will also be required to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: MPA is studying the timelines for the transition given their different power requirements and will provide an update next year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee will share more about our initiatives to support the transition for the maritime sector.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about international partnerships to catalyse our sustainability initiatives.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As a major international aviation and maritime hub, we actively support the efforts of the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to reduce emissions from international transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are also working with like-minded country partners to create sustainable international aviation and maritime ecosystems through "green lanes" for flights powered by Sustainable Aviation Fuels (SAF), as well as green and digital shipping corridors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Ng Ling Ling asked how we will encourage the aviation hub to step up its sustainability efforts.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: CAAS will be releasing more details, and I encourage companies to make full use of the funding.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More broadly, CAAS is studying the recommendations of the International Advisory Panel (IAP) on the Sustainable Air Hub and will publish the Sustainable Air Hub Blueprint in the second half of this year.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, I would now like to focus on the way forward to meet our evolving urban mobility needs, as well as the undergirding social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our COE system aims to efficiently allocate our limited vehicle quota.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Prices inevitably increase when demand is high relative to supply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The cost of Cat D COEs and its impact on motorcycle users is an issue that has been raised by Members from all sides of the House.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Besides Mr Saktiandi and the Leader of the Opposition, Ms Mariam Jaafar asked a Parliamentary Question earlier this week.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Abdul Samad did so at the end of last year, and indeed many other Members have raised this point.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And we fully understand the concern especially for those who rely on their motorcycles for their livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is why motorcycle owners receive preferential treatment under the current vehicle ownership regime.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Additional Registration Fee, Road Tax and Electronic Road Pricing (ERP) charges for motorcycles are all lower compared to other vehicle types.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And in March last year, we took additional measures to curb any speculative bidding by dealers for motorcycle COEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We halved the temporary COE (TCOE) validity period from six to three months and increased the bid deposit from $200 to $800.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More broadly, to reduce volatility in the COE cycle for all categories, we have also smoothened the supply by basing the quota on the rolling average of the de-registrations from the preceding four quarters instead of just one quarter.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Following the changes in March last year, the TCOE utilisation rates have remained high, close to 100%, in the ensuing months which reflects strong underlying demand.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is noteworthy that in the last two months, about 450 TCOEs, secured when Cat D prices were close to or above $13,000, have been forfeited along with the deposits.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, the market subsequently corrected itself with prices easing and utilisation rates going up again.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And this indicates that the system is working as intended with corrections where the market cannot support the levels of prices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This would constitute an additional 15% above the projected supply from de-registrations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Singh also suggested reviewing motorcycle financing, specifically in-house financing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They are a part of industry practice providing a service for prospective buyers.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Hire-Purchase Act provides for regulations governing such agreements.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Our agencies will take action if there is evidence of practices that contravene these regulations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Lim Biow Chuan asked about the Forward Singapore (ForwardSG) engagements that we launched in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We brought together Singaporeans from all walks of life to discuss our aspirations for future urban mobility, the trade-offs and what our renewed social compact should be.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I was heartened that many participants recognised and appreciated the improvements to our public transport system over the last decade, making it more accessible, reliable and inclusive.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about the cost of running public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: While we aspire to have a high-quality, world-class public transport system, we must also ensure financial sustainability, and this is the shared responsibility of Government, operators and commuters.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Where we land on the balance between quality, affordability and financial sustainability is driven by what we value as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We believe that commuters and taxpayers must share the financial burden equitably, because ultimately, we do not want a financially unsustainable system with a large fiscal burden for future generations of Singaporeans to bear.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Public Transport Council is reviewing the fare adjustment formula and mechanism guided by the need for a balance across these three factors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Another strong sentiment that emerged from our engagements was that inclusiveness should be at the heart of our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, we can be more inclusive in our road design.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hitherto, much of the focus in road planning has been to meet the needs of vehicular flows.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, our local streets are also an integral part of our daily lives and the pedestrian network in our communities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We use them to visit neighbourhood centres, markets, polyclinics and schools.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is where we might meet our neighbours and friends.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And there was a strong feeling amongst the dialogue participants that we should make our streets more conducive for such everyday pedestrian use, especially with an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: LTA will, therefore, pilot an initiative to design such streets with local communities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They will be called "Friendly Streets", which I think aptly captures the intent of this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Khor will elaborate on this.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Second, where at-grade road crossings are not possible, we will incorporate lifts in all new pedestrian overhead bridges (POBs) built by Government agencies where suitable and cost-effective.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In tandem, we are pressing on with our works to retrofit lifts at existing POBs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Minister of State Khor will share more on our plans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And third, in addition to pedestrians, we will also place greater emphasis on the needs of those who use active modes of transport, such as cycling.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They can expect more intra-town paths that will aid first- and last-mile connectivity to the major transportation nodes and key amenities.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For longer commutes, we are exploring cycling trunk routes to connect cyclists to more places.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey Yam Keng will give more details.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Chairman, three years ago, we were confronted by a crisis, unprecedented and unimaginable for this generation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, steeled by the experience of the pandemic and having emerged stronger, we are building for the future with optimism and confidence to drive the next bound of growth across our air, sea and land transport sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Even as the challenges and resource constraints become more complex, I would like to conclude by assuring Members that the MOT and our stakeholders and partners remain resolutely committed in our endeavour to build a resilient, sustainable and inclusive transport system for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Faisal Manap asked about bus services in Kaki Bukit.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Some of the headways are within five minutes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Commuters can also use the MyTransport app to estimate bus arrival timings and further reduce their waiting times at the bus stop.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These trips have been restored and the situation has improved.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I want to assure Mr Faisal that LTA will continue to monitor and we will introduce additional bus trips if necessary to meet higher commuter demand during peak periods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The second issue was on "Townlink feeder services".

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This was the previous name used before the Bus Contracting Model was introduced in 2016.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We now refer to such arrangements as "intra-town feeder services", where feeder services would travel around the town usually in two loops from the bus interchange.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are trade-offs to run such services, which is why they are no longer introduced for new routes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, these services often ply a much longer route, compared to a conventional hub-and-spoke model with shorter feeder services connecting different parts of the town to key transport nodes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The bus timings are, therefore, subject to more variability along the journey, which may lead to reduced reliability and longer waiting times for commuters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: About 10% of commuters use intra-town feeder services to travel to another part of the town.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The large majority of commuters use them to connect to the Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) and other bus services at key transport nodes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This means, that their commuting needs will be better served with a hub-and-spoke model instead of using the intra-town feeder services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The hub-and-spoke model is also more flexible in meeting new demand, for example, when a new Built-To-Order (BTO) estate is constructed within the town.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about City Direct Services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For City Direct Service 671 from Sengkang to Central Business District, the ridership has been increasing as more residents move into the new BTO blocks at Sengkang West.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Yeo Wan Ling asked for an update on the transport options for our workers at Tuas Port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is currently one public bus service from Tuas West Road MRT station to Tuas Port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: PSA also operates shuttle services for its staff between Tuas Port and about 50 locations across Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The MPA will form a tripartite committee with Government agencies, industry partners and unions to discuss and jointly propose practical solutions to improve accessibility to Tuas Port.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Transport (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Like waves in the ocean, the global maritime sector has experienced ups and downs over the years.
